question: What is a Pickles Stair Trencher?
answer: The Pickles Stair Trencher is a specialist woodworking machine developed for machining housings (trenches) into staircase strings. Instead of marking out and routing every tread and riser housing by hand, the machine produces accurate, repeatable housings using dedicated tooling and indexing systems. Long the UK staircase-industry standard alongside the Rayburn.

question: Who manufactured the Pickles Stair Trencher?
answer: Pickles Engineering (UK) manufactured staircase trenching machines that became widely used by staircase manufacturers throughout Britain from the mid-20th century onwards. Many machines remain in service today because of their robust cast-iron construction and mechanical simplicity — the machine has a very long useful life when properly maintained.

question: Why was the Pickles Stair Trencher revolutionary?
answer: Before dedicated trenchers, housings were cut manually using templates and routers. The Pickles machine dramatically improved accuracy, production speed, repeatability, and workshop efficiency. For many UK companies it transformed staircase production from a craft process into a semi-production process — several staircases per day became achievable in the same time it previously took to produce one.

question: How does a stair trencher work? (step by step)
answer: The operator secures the staircase string to the machine bed. The machine then positions the string, indexes to the required tread position, cuts the housing, moves to the next position, and repeats until all housings are complete. The result is a staircase string with accurately machined housings ready for assembly. Indexing is mechanical on classic machines (Pickles, Rayburn), digital on modern equivalents.

question: Why is indexing important on a stair trencher?
answer: Indexing ensures every housing is positioned consistently according to the staircase design — the machine steps between each tread position at the exact pitch and going set on the machine. Accurate indexing reduces cumulative errors across a 13-rise flight (a 1mm error compounds to 13mm at the top) and improves repeatability across identical staircases.

question: What cutter does a stair trencher use?
answer: Most trenchers use specially designed cutter heads (spiral or profile blocks) matched to the required housing dimensions — typically 32mm wide × 12-15mm deep for a standard housed string. Tooling selection depends on the staircase design, the timber species being machined, and the machine configuration. Cutter blocks are usually TCT (tungsten carbide-tipped) for hardwood work.

question: Can a Pickles stair trencher produce curved staircases?
answer: Not directly. Curved staircases have unique geometry per component — each string, tread, and riser has its own dimensions — so they generally require specialised jigs, CNC machining, or more manual methods. The Pickles is optimised for STRAIGHT flights where every housing along the string is at the same pitch angle.

question: How accurate is a Pickles stair trencher?
answer: Accuracy depends on machine condition, tool sharpness, operator setup, calibration, and maintenance. A well-maintained Pickles machine with sharp TCT tooling can consistently produce housings to ±0.3mm — more than sufficient for a housed-string joint (the wedge takes up any slack). A neglected machine with dull cutters will produce loose, burned housings that no amount of glue can rescue.

question: What timber species can a stair trencher machine?
answer: Common materials include American White Oak, European Oak, Ash, Beech, Sapele, Tulipwood, and the softwood species used for painted staircases (redwood, poplar). The correct tooling geometry and feed rates should always be selected for the material — hardwoods need slower feeds and sharper cutters, softwoods can handle faster feeds but tend to fuzz on the housing walls if the cutter isn't clean.

question: How long does stair trencher setup take?
answer: Setup time varies with the staircase design and tooling — usually 15-40 minutes to configure indexing, fit the correct cutter block, and set housing depth. Once configured, the same setup can often be used to machine multiple identical staircases in sequence — this is why the trencher is so efficient for medium-to-large production runs but less compelling for single bespoke jobs.

question: Why do factories keep one operator on the stair trencher?
answer: Experienced operators become highly familiar with the machine's sounds, cutter wear, feed rates, setup adjustments, and small changes in cut quality. That experience improves consistency and productivity — a stair trencher run by a rotating pool of operators typically produces more variation than the same machine run by one dedicated operator over months and years.

question: How long can a Pickles stair trencher last?
answer: Many industrial woodworking machines remain productive for decades when properly maintained — Pickles machines from the 1970s and 1980s are still in daily use in UK workshops today. Cast-iron frames, hardened steel indexing, and mechanically-simple drivetrains all contribute to longevity. Bearings and belts are wear parts; the frame effectively lasts forever.

question: Why is my stair trencher burning the housing walls?
answer: Possible causes: dull cutters (most common), resin build-up on the cutter face, feed rate too slow (cutter dwells and heats the timber), or incorrect spindle speed for the material. Fix: sharpen or replace cutters, clean resin with a proper solvent, increase feed rate slightly, and confirm spindle RPM matches the tooling spec.

question: Why is the housing surface rough after trenching?
answer: Possible causes: blunt tooling, machine vibration, loose bearings on the spindle or feed rollers, incorrect cutter geometry for the timber species, or feed rate too fast. Diagnostic sequence: touch the cutter (safely, machine off) — if it drags a finger, it needs sharpening. If it's sharp, tighten spindle bearings and confirm the workpiece is clamped rigidly.

question: Why is every housing on my strings getting progressively wider?
answer: Possible causes: cutter wear (block is losing material with each pass), loose spindle allowing sideways movement, incorrect setup with the workpiece drifting, or tool movement in the collet. Fix: check cutter dimensions with a calliper, tighten spindle bearings + confirm collet is clean and torqued, and verify the workpiece clamping isn't slipping.

question: Why aren't the housings on my staircase strings lining up correctly?
answer: Possible causes: incorrect indexing (mechanical index worn or misadjusted), wrong setup dimensions on the pitch/going gauges, workpiece movement between cuts (clamping insufficient), or calibration error accumulating across the flight. Fix: re-calibrate the indexing mechanism against a machined reference block, verify setup dimensions match the drawing, and check clamping pressure on the string.

question: What daily and weekly maintenance does a stair trencher need?
answer: DAILY (before starting production): check emergency stop, check cutter security, check guards, remove dust and shavings, lubricate specified moving parts, verify machine settings against the drawing, inspect dust extraction, and make a test cut. WEEKLY: clean resin from tooling, inspect bearings, check drive belts, tighten fixings, verify stops and indexing mechanism, test lubrication points, check cutter balance. Log every check — a maintenance record is a defensive document if a housing fails inspection.

question: Would a modern staircase factory buy another Pickles Stair Trencher today?
answer: If a workshop mainly produces standard straight staircases and has access to a well-maintained machine, yes — a Pickles trencher is still a practical production tool with excellent cost-per-string economics. For businesses producing a wide variety of bespoke, curved, or highly customised staircases, modern CNC machining centres offer much greater flexibility. Many successful UK manufacturers combine dedicated staircase machinery WITH CNC, using each where it provides the greatest benefit rather than replacing one with the other.

question: What is a staircase routing jig?
answer: A staircase routing jig is a precision template that guides a handheld plunge router to cut accurate tread and riser housings into staircase strings. Before CNC became widespread, thousands of UK staircases were produced using routing jigs, and many bespoke staircase companies still use them today for one-off and low-volume work.

question: Why use a routing jig instead of measuring and routing every housing separately?
answer: A jig eliminates repeated measuring. Once positioned correctly, every housing is cut to the same width, depth, angle, and position along the string. This improves consistency dramatically and reduces the chance of operator error — the jig enforces geometry the operator would otherwise have to hand-transfer from the drawing every time.

question: What is the biggest advantage of a router jig over a dedicated stair trencher?
answer: Flexibility. Unlike a stair trencher (which is optimised for standard housings), a router jig can be adapted for different staircase designs with relatively simple adjustments — different pitches, different string widths, different housing profiles. This makes the jig particularly useful for custom and bespoke work where each staircase differs from the last.

question: Who typically uses staircase routing jigs?
answer: Small joinery shops, bespoke staircase manufacturers, carpenter-builders, renovation specialists, and restoration companies. Any workshop where staircases are a regular but not high-volume output — the jig gives close to trencher accuracy without the capital investment or floor space of a dedicated machine.

question: Can a router jig produce factory-quality staircase strings?
answer: Yes. With a well-made jig, sharp cutters, and careful setup, results indistinguishable from a stair trencher are achievable. The quality depends on the accuracy of the jig, the condition of the router (spindle runout, base flatness), and the skill of the operator (consistent feed rate, correct plunge depth). A tired jig with a worn guide bush will produce worse results than a Pickles trencher — the jig must be maintained too.

question: Why use a plunge router (rather than a fixed-base router) for staircase housings?
answer: Because the cutter starts INSIDE the timber, not from an edge. Plunge routers let you lower the spinning cutter into a housing at any position on the string, produce clean housings without needing an exposed edge for entry, are easy to control at plunge depth, and work well with templates + guide bushes. Fixed-base routers can't safely start a cut mid-material.

question: Which router brands are popular for professional staircase work?
answer: Professional workshops commonly use routers from Festool, Makita, DeWalt, Bosch Professional, and Trend — all of which produce plunge routers with the power, base flatness, and dust extraction that stair housing work needs. Choice depends on workshop preference, available accessories (guide bushes, templates), and local service support. All of the above will do the job well when paired with quality cutters.

question: What router cutters are used for staircase housing work?
answer: Common choices: straight cutters (simplest, cheapest, work well for standard housings), spiral up-cut cutters (better chip evacuation, cleaner cut in hardwoods), spiral compression cutters (clean top AND bottom edge — best for laminated or veneered strings), carbide-tipped cutters (long-lasting, good general purpose), and solid-carbide cutters (premium — best cut quality, highest cost per cutter).

question: Why are carbide cutters preferred for staircase routing?
answer: Carbide stays sharp much longer than HSS steel, produces cleaner cuts, handles hardwoods (oak, walnut, ash) without dulling quickly, and reduces workshop downtime for sharpening. The higher upfront cost is repaid many times over in longer service life + better housing quality — HSS cutters have essentially disappeared from professional workshops.

question: What is a router guide bush?
answer: A guide bush fits to the base of the router and follows the edge of a template or jig. The cutter remains centred inside the guide bush, and the guide bush controls the path the cutter follows across the workpiece. Without the correct guide bush, the housing size will be inaccurate — the router will cut wherever the base wanders.

question: Why is guide bush size critical for router jig accuracy?
answer: The guide bush size determines the OFFSET between the cutter and the template edge. Changing the guide bush changes that offset, which changes the finished housing dimensions. Even a 1mm difference in guide bush diameter shifts the housing edge by 0.5mm — enough to produce loose or tight-fitting joints. Every jig is designed around a specific cutter + guide bush combination and swapping either invalidates the jig geometry.

question: What is router cutter offset (guide bush maths)?
answer: Offset is the distance between the outside of the guide bush and the cutting edge — it's how far away from the template edge the router will actually cut. Formula: offset = (guide_bush_diameter - cutter_diameter) / 2. Every staircase jig is designed around one specific cutter + guide bush combination, and the template is dimensioned assuming that exact offset.

question: Why should you test-cut before machining the actual staircase strings?
answer: Professional workshops always machine a test piece to confirm housing width, housing depth, cutter offset, jig alignment, and surface finish. A five-minute test cut can prevent wasting expensive timber — a full oak string is often £80-150 of stock, and one wrong-setup pass can ruin it. Test on offcut of the same species so the cutter behaves identically.

question: What mistakes do beginners make with router jigs on staircase work?
answer: Common errors: using blunt cutters (biggest cause of poor housings), incorrect guide bush size for the template, poor clamping (jig or workpiece moves mid-cut), routing too quickly (tear-out) or too slowly (burning), forgetting to clear chips between passes (re-cutting the same chips causes burning and dull cutters), and measuring from the wrong reference point on the jig.

question: Why does my router chatter during housing cuts?
answer: Possible causes: loose guide bush, worn bearings in the router spindle, dull cutter, feed rate too fast for the cutter geometry, inadequate workpiece support (string sagging in the middle), or poor clamping letting the router lift. Fix: tighten guide bush, check spindle bearings, sharpen or replace cutter, slow the feed slightly, support the string every 500mm, and clamp with even downward pressure.

question: Why does my router cutter burn the timber in staircase housings?
answer: Possible causes: resin build-up on the cutter (most common on oak), blunt tooling, feed rate too slow (cutter dwells and generates heat), excessive spindle speed for the cutter, or re-cutting chips that didn't clear from the previous pass. Fix: clean resin with solvent, sharpen the cutter, feed slightly faster, drop RPM if the cutter spec allows, and ensure dust extraction is running to clear chips.

question: Why is one housing wider than the others on my staircase string?
answer: Possible causes: loose template (jig has moved between housings), loose guide bush (has slipped in the router base), cutter movement (collet slipped), worn bearings letting the cutter wobble, or the operator lifting the router during the cut. Fix: re-clamp the jig, retighten guide bush, check the collet, replace bearings if runout is measurable, and practice keeping consistent downward pressure through the plunge.

question: How often should router cutters be replaced?
answer: No fixed interval — replace or sharpen when you notice burning marks, increased cutting effort, rough housing surfaces, tear-out at the housing edges, excessive cutter noise, or generally poor finish. Track cutter life per material — a spiral carbide cutter in oak may last 100+ housings; the same cutter in a resinous softwood may need cleaning after 20. Set a diary reminder to inspect cutters weekly.

question: What is the first step when manufacturing a staircase?
answer: Everything begins with accurate site measurements. The manufacturer confirms the floor-to-floor height, opening size (stairwell width and length), wall positions, landing arrangement, and any obstacles (RSJs, ceiling beams, doors that open into the stair area) before the staircase is designed. A wrong site measurement causes remakes — every professional workshop verifies measurements before production begins, particularly on bespoke work.
